newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission agrees land plan environment rules.
newsitem.headline: Commission agrees land plan environment rules.

text.p: Land-use decisions related to energy, waste, mining and transport plans in the European Union will not be cleared until their environmental impact has been assessed, according to draft rules from the European Commission.
The Commission, which agreed the proposal on Wednesday, said the move would strengthen the EU's existing system for assessing the environmental impact of projects.

"By taking environmental consequences into account at an earlier stage of the planning process, the Commission's new draft directive will increase environmental protection and reduce economic impact for operators," it said in a statement.

Existing EU law, based on Directive 85/377/EEC and under revision in the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament, COM(93)575, requires environmental assessments only for specific projects in specific locations, identifying perhaps the environmental effects of a road bypass or a new dam or bridge.
Parliament said last month that planned revisions to the 1985 EIA directive should be stricter than those adopted in the Council's common position of June 1996.

While non-compliance with even these rules by many of the EU's 15 countries has led to some high-profile clashes with the executive, an underlying problem has been that assessements at project level can miss the bigger picture of say an entire road development project or a series of mineral extraction sites.

The Commission said an early examination of land-use plans and programmes, before the development of detailed projects, would save developers time and money and would allow for alternatives to be considered.
"The costs associated with this type of assessment, on the other hand, is marginal compared to the scale of investments required," the statement said.

Commission official Christine Dalby told a news conference that no EU members had equivalent assessment procedures at present although Spain, France, Finland and the Netherlands had partial ones and others carried out checks informally.

"None of the existing land-use planning systems adequately cover the minimum requirements of a strategic environmental assessment. The (proposal) will ensure that minimum requirements are met in all countries," the statement said.
The proposed directive, which requires EU member state and European Parliament approval before becoming law, is slated in a Commission paper to come into force by October 2000.

The proposal was adopted as a draft directive under Article 130s paragraph 1, meaning that it will require a qualified majority vote in Council rather than unanimity, as had been considered in recent meetings within the Commission.
